choices.text: United SFO-DEN-OMA, departs 2:10 p.m. and arrives 8:55 p.m., 82-minute Denver layover, $415, with a free window currently available.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Without history, the choices present unresolved tradeoffs among an earlier arrival, a lower fare, a midafternoon departure, and a later departure. History supplies both the afternoon default and the soft United tie-breaker needed to put A first.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the 2:10 p.m. United departure.
probes.label_rationale: A is an ordinary, workable afternoon departure and is only $5 above the comparably timed Delta line. The afternoon default distinguishes it from the morning and evening options, while the soft United preference reasonably breaks the close A-versus-C comparison without overriding a material fare, routing, or timing advantage.
probes.query: Jonah is preparing a no-booking shortlist for a Monday SFO-to-Omaha outbound before a Tuesday 11:00 a.m. internal review. Monday is otherwise open, the hotel will hold a late arrival, and each regular-economy option has one comfortable connection. Which outbound should lead the shortlist?

choices.text: United SFO-ORD-IND, departs 1:50 p.m. and arrives 9:15 p.m., 81-minute Chicago layover, $414; a no-fee aisle is selectable now, while a window is not currently open.
United SFO-ORD-IND, departs 9:35 a.m. and arrives 6:55 p.m., 84-minute Chicago layover, $407; a no-fee window is selectable now.
United SFO-ORD-IND, departs 10:55 a.m. and arrives 7:30 p.m., 78-minute Chicago layover, $410; a no-fee window is selectable now.
United SFO-ORD-IND, departs 6:05 p.m. and arrives 11:20 p.m., 86-minute Chicago layover, $403; a no-fee window is selectable now.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The query alone does not establish whether a free window, a modest fare saving, an earlier arrival, or a later daytime departure should prevail. The answer requires applying the scoped afternoon preference while treating the window preference as a lower-priority seat-specific consideration.
probes.gold_action: Rank the 1:50 p.m. United option first and request a window later if one becomes available without a fee.
probes.label_rationale: A is the only ordinary afternoon option that avoids a very late arrival. Jonah's afternoon-departure preference is stronger than the background window-seat preference, so the lack of a currently free window is a seat-selection follow-up rather than a reason to favor a morning option. The small fare differences do not make A materially worse.
probes.query: Jonah is traveling alone from SFO to Indianapolis on Monday for a Tuesday 11:00 a.m. site briefing. Monday has no local commitment, every option is regular economy with one comfortable connection, and each arrival permits a normal hotel check-in. Which outbound should be ranked first?

probes.difficulty_rationale: All four choices support the next-day session. The query leaves unresolved whether to optimize for fare, earlier arrival, a later departure, carrier, or connection length; history is needed to recognize why A's modest combined preference advantages justify leading with it.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the 2:15 p.m. United itinerary through Denver.
probes.label_rationale: A combines the afternoon departure default with United's soft positive weight and a shorter comfortable connection. C is a viable, lower-cost afternoon alternative, but its $8 saving is small relative to the combined carrier and connection advantages; B is a close morning United alternative rather than the default first look.
probes.query: Jonah is making a no-booking Monday outbound shortlist from SFO to Fargo for a Tuesday 10:30 a.m. distributor session. He has no Monday commitment, the hotel accepts late arrivals, and every itinerary is regular economy with one legal domestic connection. Which line should lead?

probes.difficulty_rationale: The prompt creates a genuine conflict between preserving the afternoon default and arriving in time for an optional client event. No generic rule establishes how much the dinner is worth relative to schedule and fare, and history is needed to avoid treating an optional event as an automatic override.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the 2:00 p.m. United option and note that it does not assume attendance at the optional dinner.
probes.label_rationale: The dinner is useful but expressly optional, so it is not a stronger meeting-driven requirement that displaces Jonah's normal afternoon-departure default. B also retains the soft United preference. A is a sensible alternative only if Jonah decides the dinner should become a current-trip priority; D is the closest afternoon alternative but gives up United for a modest saving and a later arrival.
probes.query: Jonah is considering Monday SFO-to-Oklahoma City travel for a Tuesday 10:00 a.m. working session. A distributor has invited him to an optional 6:45 p.m. dinner; Jonah says being there would be useful, but attendance is not required and the substantive work starts Tuesday. Monday is otherwise open, and each regular-economy option has one comfortable connection. Which outbound should lead the recommendation?

United SFO-ORD-PIA, departs 11:00 a.m. and arrives 7:35 p.m., 85-minute Chicago layover, $415.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The alternatives distribute the relevant benefits across time of day, fare, carrier, layover length, and arrival time. The query does not state how to weigh those factors, so selecting A requires combining the departure-time default with the separate carrier and connection preferences.
probes.gold_action: List the 2:15 p.m. United itinerary first.
probes.label_rationale: A is an afternoon United departure with a short, comfortable single connection. B preserves the carrier and connection advantages but gives up the afternoon default; C preserves an afternoon departure but adds a substantially longer layover; D is cheaper but shifts into an evening departure and a much later arrival. None of those differences is a material generic defeat of A.
probes.query: Jonah is preparing a Monday SFO-to-Peoria shortlist for a Tuesday 10:00 a.m. plant review. There are no Monday obligations, the hotel accepts late arrivals, and all options are regular economy with one connection. Which itinerary should be listed first?

choices.text: Lead with United SFO-DEN-ELP, departing 10:15 a.m. and arriving 6:20 p.m., 78-minute Denver layover, $425, on the assumption that Jonah needs to attend the handoff.
Lead with United SFO-DEN-ELP, departing 2:20 p.m. and arriving 9:10 p.m., 82-minute Denver layover, $412, and omit the handoff.
Hold both United options, keep the 2:20 p.m. flight as the provisional afternoon line, and ask whether the 8:00 p.m. handoff requires Jonah in person before moving to a morning departure.
Lead with Delta SFO-SLC-ELP, departing 12:05 p.m. and arriving 7:55 p.m., 80-minute Salt Lake City layover, $403, as a compromise.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A generic planner could reasonably assume the handoff matters, ignore it, or choose the nominal compromise. History supplies the specific procedural rule: do not abandon the afternoon default for a possibly conflicting constraint until Jonah confirms that the constraint should control.
probes.gold_action: Keep the afternoon United option provisional, hold the earlier United alternative, and ask whether the handoff is mandatory before broadening to a morning departure.
probes.label_rationale: The possible handoff creates an unresolved same-day constraint, but it is not yet confirmed as a requirement. Jonah's departure-time default calls for an afternoon first look, while its exception calls for confirmation before unilaterally broadening to an earlier time window when another stated constraint may conflict. C preserves both viable plans without treating either priority as settled.
probes.query: Jonah is drafting, but not booking, Monday SFO-to-El Paso travel. The customer may hold an 8:00 p.m. installation handoff at the hotel, which is 20 minutes from the airport; the customer will confirm tomorrow whether Jonah must attend. Jonah says he would prefer to join if it occurs but has not said whether that should outweigh a later departure. Tuesday's first required event is at 10:00 a.m. Which recommendation should lead the draft?

choices.text: Assign 18B to Jonah and 18C to Priya so they sit together, with Jonah in a middle seat and Priya on an aisle.
Assign 12A to Jonah and 14C to Priya, giving Jonah a window and Priya an aisle in separate rows.
Assign 16C to Jonah and 16D to Priya, placing them across the aisle in the same row but giving neither a window.
Leave both seats unassigned until check-in in case a different adjacent pair opens.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Without history, adjacency, same-row proximity, and separation are all defensible workplace-travel conventions. The decisive fact is the scope of Jonah's window preference when no companion-seating need exists, combined with Priya's separate aisle preference.
probes.gold_action: Assign Jonah the available window and Priya the available aisle in separate rows.
probes.label_rationale: The shared reservation does not create a companion-seating need: Priya expressly does not require adjacency and receives her preferred aisle in B. Jonah's flight-seat preference can therefore apply to his own selectable seat. It should not be transformed into a rule that group-booked coworkers must sit together or that seat selection should be deferred without reason.
probes.query: Jonah and Priya are on the same employer reservation to a training, but they will work separately. Priya says an aisle would be nice and that she does not care whether they sit together. Standard seats are free. Which seat assignment should be used?

Delta SFO-MSP-DSM, departs 2:15 p.m. and arrives 9:00 p.m., 79-minute Minneapolis layover, $404; a free window seat is selectable now.

Southwest OAK-DEN-DSM, departs 4:50 p.m. and arrives 10:20 p.m., 80-minute Denver layover, $393; boarding position rather than a seat assignment is available now.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The query alone leaves a close tradeoff among a visible window, earlier versus later arrival, modest fare differences, airport choice, and carrier. History is needed to recognize that a deferred seat map is a limitation to manage, not a reason to extend the window preference into a carrier-selection rule.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the United itinerary, note that advance seat selection is unavailable, and request a window as soon as online check-in opens.
probes.label_rationale: Jonah's window preference governs seat selection, not whether an otherwise comparable itinerary must be rejected because its seat map opens later. A retains the soft United preference and an earlier arrival than B; the proper follow-up is to seek a window at the first available selection opportunity, rather than treating B's currently visible window as determinative.
probes.query: Jonah is traveling alone to Des Moines for a Tuesday 10:00 a.m. meeting. All options are regular economy with one comfortable connection, and every arrival is workable. Which line should lead the no-booking shortlist?

choices.text: Request an exterior city-view king with an in-room coffee maker but no refrigerator or mini-fridge.
Request a courtyard-facing king with both an in-room coffee maker and a refrigerator or mini-fridge.
Request an exterior city-view king with a refrigerator or mini-fridge but no in-room coffee maker.
Request any available room with a view rather than specifying room amenities.

probes.difficulty_rationale: With rate, quality, cancellation, location, and dining held equal, the query alone does not say whether a room view or a particular amenity bundle matters more. The answer requires enforcing the seat-preference boundary while applying the separate, relevant hotel-room amenity preference.
probes.gold_action: Request the courtyard-facing room with both the coffee maker and refrigerator or mini-fridge.
probes.label_rationale: A flight window-seat preference is limited to flight seat location and does not create a preference for a hotel-room view. For a multi-night work stay, the relevant established room criteria are the coffee maker and refrigerator or mini-fridge, both of which B provides.
probes.query: Jonah is selecting a four-night solo work-hotel room near the plant. Each room is the same price, refundable, equally close to the site, and at the same 4.3-rated hotel with nearby dining. He has not requested a view. Which room request should be placed on the booking?
